evidence.locator: Abstract; Fig. 1 caption and the passage after it

opening.text: About 66 million years ago, a mass extinction marked the end of the Cretaceous Period.
An estimated three-quarters of species were lost, including every dinosaur that was not a bird.
At that time a large asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, forming the Chicxulub crater, now buried beneath younger rock.
Renne and colleagues (2013) reported dating that places the impact and the extinction within 32,000 years of each other.
That figure is a limit on how far apart the two could be, not a measured gap between them.
At two sites in the western United States, researchers identified the boundary by shock-altered minerals, an unusual enrichment in iridium, and the disappearance of fossil pollen and spores.

image.alt: Colour relief map of the north-west corner of the Yucatán Peninsula. A dashed semicircle labelled "Trough" curves inland from the coast. Arrows labelled "Cenotes (sinkholes)" point to small pits along it.
image.caption: Radar height map of the north-west Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico, with NASA's labels. The dashed line follows a shallow trough, 3 to 5 metres deep and about 5 kilometres wide, which NASA describes as a surface expression of the buried crater's outer boundary. Sinkholes (cenotes) are marked along it. Heights are greatly exaggerated. This is a rendering of elevation measurements, not a photograph of the crater. Data: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, February 2000.
